findings.summary: Page titles lag their contents by roughly one page, so a learner navigating by title lands on the wrong material.
findings.evidence: Page 5 is titled "Tagged Unions & Predicates" but contains no tagged-union blocks (it opens with "4. Your Own Guards" and ends in `asserts`); page 6 "Predicate Risk & asserts" contains `never` ("1. The Bottom Type", "2. assertNever") while predicate risk ("1. Promises, Not Proofs") sits on page 5; page 8 "Choosing A Guard" contains the breakage material ("4. Callbacks Lose It", "5. let vs const", "6. Calls & Aliases") while page 9 is titled "Where Narrowing Breaks".
findings.fix: Retitle each page to the topic that actually dominates its blocks (e.g. page 5 → "Predicates: Writing Your Own Guards", page 6 → "asserts & never", page 8 → "Choosing A Guard & Where It Breaks"), or re-cut the page boundaries so each title's topic starts on that page.

findings.summary: Page 1 shows an exhaustive `switch` over a discriminated union calling `assertNever`, three concepts that are not introduced until pages 4 and 6.
findings.evidence: Page 1 code block: "switch (s.kind) {", "case 'circle': return circle(s);", "default: return assertNever(s); // errors" — `s`/`Shape` and tag checking are first defined on page 4 ("4. Discriminated Unions"), and `assertNever` on page 6 ("2. assertNever").
findings.fix: Move this code block to page 6 beside the `assertNever` definition; if page 1 needs a preview of the payoff, replace it with the `pad()` typeof example already on the page or a one-line teaser under "5. The Five Tools" that names `never` without showing unexplained code.

findings.summary: A `Result<T, E>` code block is dropped on page 1 with no heading, no bullets, and no later explanation anywhere in the handbook.
findings.evidence: Page 1 code block: "type Result<T, E> = | { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };", "if (r.ok) use(r.value); else log(r.error);" — no surrounding text explains it, and no later page mentions the Result pattern (page 6 only says "return a discriminated result instead").
findings.fix: Remove the block from page 1 and place it on page 9 with a short heading ("The Result Pattern") plus a bullet stating that narrowing on `ok` replaces try/catch and makes error handling exhaustive.

findings.summary: Page 2 opens with a code block that narrows `s: Shape` on `s.kind`, but `Shape` and discriminant narrowing are not defined until page 4.
findings.evidence: First block of page 2: "function area(s: Shape) {", "if (s.kind === 'circle')", "return Math.PI * s.r ** 2; // s.r: number" — the `Shape` alias is first declared on page 4 ("type Shape = | { kind: 'circle'; r: number } ...").
findings.fix: Swap this opener for a `typeof`- or early-return-based example that matches page 2's actual topic (terminators and loops), and keep the `area(s: Shape)` snippet on page 4 under "1. switch On The Tag".

findings.summary: The claim that `typeof v === k` narrows when `k` holds a string-literal type is wrong — TypeScript only applies typeof narrowing when the compared operand is a syntactic string literal.
findings.evidence: Slide 3, "6. Functions & Literals": "The compared string must be a literal type." / "`const k = 'string'; typeof v === k` narrows only if k is literal." TypeScript 5.9 checker: `if (left.kind === TypeOfExpression && isStringLiteralLike(right)) return narrowTypeByTypeof(...)` — `isStringLiteralLike` is a syntax-node test (StringLiteral / no-substitution template), so an identifier of type `'string'` never reaches `narrowTypeByTypeof`.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "The compared string must be written as a literal in place — `const k = 'string'; typeof v === k` does NOT narrow, even though `k` has the literal type `'string'`." (Note the contrast with equality/discriminant narrowing on slide 9, where a literal-typed const DOES narrow, because that path uses the operand's type rather than its syntax.)

findings.summary: Page 3 teaches `instanceof`-based error handling before page 4 explains what `instanceof` does.
findings.evidence: Page 3 ends with "`instanceof` is the standard way to make them usable", heading "2. Canonical Use: Errors" and the `catch (e) { if (e instanceof HttpError) ... }` block; page 4 then opens with "1. How instanceof Works" — "`x instanceof C` narrows x to C at runtime. It checks `C.prototype` against x's prototype chain."
findings.fix: Move the `catch`/`unknown` bullets, the "2. Canonical Use: Errors" heading and its try/catch block onto page 4 after "1. How instanceof Works", so the mechanism precedes its canonical use.

findings.summary: The `isDefined` guard is typed `v: T | null`, so it does not remove `undefined` from the resulting type even though the runtime check does.
findings.evidence: Slide 5, "5. Two Big Uses": "function isDefined<T>(v: T | null): v is T {" / "  return v != null;   // kills undefined too". For `list: (string | undefined)[]`, inference gives `T = string | undefined`, so `list.filter(isDefined)` is typed `(string | undefined)[]` — the comment's promise holds at runtime but not in the type.
findings.fix: Change the signature to `function isDefined<T>(v: T | null | undefined): v is T`, so `T` is inferred without the nullish members and `filter` really yields `T[]`.

findings.summary: The claim that a check on `arr[0]` does not narrow a later `arr[0]` is false — element access with a literal index is a narrowable reference in TypeScript, and the stated reason (mutation) is not why.
findings.evidence: Slide 9, "2. Positions That Slip": "`if (arr[0] === 'x')` does not narrow a later `arr[0]`." / "TS cannot prove the array was not mutated in between." TypeScript 5.9 `isMatchingReference` handles `ElementAccessExpression` via `getAccessedPropertyName` → `tryGetElementAccessExpressionName`, which accepts `isStringOrNumericLiteralLike(node.argumentExpression)`; so `arr[0]` after `if (arr[0] === 'x')` is narrowed to `'x'`.
findings.fix: Replace with the accurate version: `arr[0]` (and `obj[key]` for a literal-typed const key) DOES narrow, and — exactly like the property case on slide 8 — the narrowing is unsound: an intervening `arr.push()`/`splice()`/call does not re-widen it. Use the slot for the genuinely non-narrowing case instead, e.g. `arr[i]` with a mutable `i`, or `arr.find(...)` results.

findings.summary: The acronym CFA is used as a heading and reused on page 2 without ever being expanded.
findings.evidence: Page 1 heading "6. CFA In One Look"; page 2 bullet "CFA iterates back-edges to a fixed point." — the words "Control Flow Analysis" appear nowhere in the content.
findings.fix: Change the page 1 heading to "6. Control Flow Analysis (CFA)" so the first use defines the abbreviation.

findings.summary: The `typeof` section is closed out on page 2 and then reopened on page 3 after an unrelated truthiness section, splitting one topic in two.
findings.evidence: Page 2 states "1. Where typeof Stops — Covers primitives plus function and object. Nothing more." and then moves to "2. Truthiness"; page 3 then returns to typeof with "6. Functions & Literals — `typeof x === 'function'` picks the callable union members" and "The compared string must be a literal type."
findings.fix: Move "6. Functions & Literals" up to page 2 immediately after "4. typeof Strings"/"5. The typeof null Trap", so "Where typeof Stops" genuinely ends the typeof coverage before truthiness begins.

findings.summary: Type-predicate and utility-type notation is used on page 2 before either is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "Arrays are objects too — use `Array.isArray(x)` (`x is any[]`)" and "`else` of `typeof x === 'string'` gets `Exclude<T, string>`" — the `x is T` form is first explained on page 5 ("Return type is `param is Type`") and `Exclude` on page 7 ("==Exclude== is the same for the `else` branch").
findings.fix: On page 2 drop the parenthetical `x is any[]` (say "a built-in guard" and forward-reference page 5) and phrase the else branch as "the union minus the matched members", saving `Exclude<T, string>` for page 7.

findings.summary: The TS 4.9 `in` improvement is attributed to the wrong branch — it made the positive branch narrow unlisted properties, not the negative branch.
findings.evidence: Slide 3, "5. The in Operator": "TS 4.9+ narrows the negative branch better." TypeScript 4.9 release notes: "TypeScript 4.9 makes the `in` operator a little bit more powerful when narrowing types that don't list the property at all. Instead of leaving them as-is, the language will intersect their types with `Record<"property-key-being-checked", unknown>`" — i.e. the true branch (`unknown` → `object & Record<"name", unknown>`).
findings.fix: Replace the bullet with: "TS 4.9+: `'k' in obj` on a type that doesn't declare `k` narrows the TRUE branch to `obj & Record<'k', unknown>` — which is what makes `typeof v.id === 'string'` compile after `'id' in v`."

findings.summary: Section numbers run out of sequence across several pages, so the numbering gives a reader no reliable reading order.
findings.evidence: Page 3 runs "6. Functions & Literals" → "3. The != null Idiom" → "4. Equality Narrowing"; page 4 runs "1. How instanceof Works" → "3. Where It Fails" (its "2." is on page 3) and later "1. switch On The Tag" → "3. Async State, Modelled" → "2. Keep Tags Literal"; page 5 runs "4. asserts Signatures" → "3. TS 5.5 Inference"; page 8 runs "3. Escape Hatch Ranking" → "2. Decision Rules".
findings.fix: Renumber headings so each page's numbers ascend in reading order and no section's number precedes an earlier-numbered section on a later page — in particular reorder page 4 to 1/2/3 and page 5 so "3. TS 5.5 Inference" closes the predicate run before "4. asserts Signatures".

findings.summary: The red pushpin graphic for the yellow annotation note is drawn on top of the code line, obscuring characters in the middle of the type expression.
findings.evidence: In the code block containing "type Rest = Exclude<Shape,Circle>;" the pushpin icon sits directly over the glyphs between "Shape," and "Circle", with the note "same tag, at the type level" pinned below it.
findings.fix: Offset the pushpin anchor so it sits in the blank gutter below the last code line (or move the sticky note's anchor point to the right margin) instead of overlapping the code text.

findings.summary: The claim that `any` yields no useful narrowed type is wrong — typeof, instanceof and predicate guards all narrow `any` to the checked type.
findings.evidence: Slide 8, "3. any Is The Enemy": "`any` passes every guard and yields no useful narrowed type." TypeScript 5.9 `narrowTypeByTypeName` special-cases `any` only for `"object"` and `"function"` (`return type.flags & Any ? type : ...`); for `'string'`/`'number'`/etc. it substitutes the implied primitive, so `function f(x: any) { if (typeof x === 'string') { /* x: string */ } }` really narrows.
findings.fix: Restate the actual problem: `any` narrows fine inside a guard, but the compiler never FORCES a guard — any unchecked access on `any` also compiles. Then keep the existing advice to type untrusted input as `unknown`.

findings.summary: The red pushpin graphic for the yellow annotation note overlaps the trailing comment line of the satisfies code block.
findings.evidence: In the block "} satisfies Shape;  // kind stays" / "// checked, but never widened", the pushpin icon for the note "as Shape would widen the tag" is drawn over the end of the "never widened" comment line.
findings.fix: Add vertical padding between the last code line and the pinned note, or anchor the pin outside the code block's text column.
